Aten. The sun disk elevated to supreme and sole divinity by the revolutionary pharaoh Akhenaten. Rather than worshipping Ra or other traditional gods, Akhenaten promoted exclusive devotion to the Aten as the universal creative force. Depicted as the sun disk itself with rays extending downward, each ray ending in a hand, the Aten represented a stark departure from the anthropomorphic divine imagery of traditional Egyptian religion. Akhenaten ruled from around thirteen fifty-three to thirteen thirty-six BCE during the eighteenth dynasty, and he elevated the Aten to supreme status during his reign. This represented a fundamental break with traditional polytheism. Akhenaten promoted the Aten as the sole and universal god, an early form of monotheism unprecedented in Egyptian religion. The life-giving rays of the Aten were believed to sustain all creation. The disk itself was the visible manifestation of divine power. Worship of the Aten took place through direct praise and adoration of the sun disk in the open air, rejecting the temple imagery and conventional priesthoods of traditional Egyptian religion. After Akhenaten's death, traditional worship of Ra and other gods was quickly restored. The Aten cult was abandoned and suppressed. Akhenaten had moved Egypt's capital to Akhetaten, in modern-day Tell el-Amarna, a purpose-built city dedicated entirely to Aten worship. With the restoration of traditional religion, this city was abandoned as well. Some scholars have theorized that the Aten cult may have influenced later monotheistic religions, though the connection remains speculative and debated.
